"I taught her that a little dab will do," says the actress, who stars in the ABC comedy *Miss Guided*. "She's going to wear makeup regardless, so she might as well learn to do it well."

**Did you pick up any makeup tricks during your modeling days?**
One of my favorites is applying white pencil along the inner lower lid—it creates that wide-awake look instantly. **What's the one makeup item you can't live without?**
I'm devoted to Revlon ColorStay foundation. I can do absolutely anything while wearing it, and it stays put all day. It also contains sunscreen and gives my skin a wonderfully natural glow. It really does cover everything.

**You've gone back and forth between blonde and brunette. Which do you prefer?**
My natural color is dark blonde, but at the moment I'm enjoying being a brunette. Last summer I did a film that required platinum blonde hair, and I absolutely hated it. # Brooke Burns Shares Her Beauty Secrets

At age 9, while dreaming of becoming a professional dancer, Brooke Burns had a rather heavy-handed relationship with cosmetics. "I used to swipe my mother's Borghese red lipstick and slather it on like a circus performer!" she recalls. "And nothing beats a cheap black eyeliner for creating a smoldering gaze." Now 29 and raising her 7-year-old daughter alone, the actress—currently appearing on ABC's "Miss Guided"—focuses on teaching restraint rather than excess. "My motto for her is 'less is more,'" Burns explains. "Since she's determined to wear makeup regardless, I figure she might as well learn the right way."

**Did your modeling career teach you any beauty hacks?**
One trick I swear by is lining the inner lower lid with white pencil—it instantly brightens the eyes. When I'm pressed for time at night, I skip the fancy routine and just layer on mascara with black pencil around the entire rim. Takes ninety seconds and gives you serious sex appeal.

**What product could you never give up?**
Revlon Color Stay foundation is my ride-or-die. It handles whatever I throw at it during the day and doesn't budge. The built-in SPF gives my skin this effortless radiance too, and it hides absolutely everything.

**You've gone back and forth between blonde and brunette hair. Which suits you better?**
Naturally, I'm a dark blonde, though brunette is my current favorite. Last summer, for a film role, they bleached my hair platinum blonde and I couldn't stand it. Since I already have a strong personality, combining that with blonde hair made me seem superficial to people. Going darker shifts attention toward my actual face instead of just my hair color.

**What's your routine for maintaining dyed hair?**
Nothing compares to L'Oréal's Nature's Therapy Mega Moisture Nurturing shampoo—my stylist introduced me to it and I've been hooked ever since. I've also discovered Paul Mitchell's Fudge Brownie shade, which works wonders. People constantly tell me my hair looks incredibly healthy.

**Was good hair always part of your look?**
Absolutely not! High school me was obsessed with volume—hot rollers, teasing, the whole nine yards, complete with those cringeworthy mall bangs. Between dance rehearsals, I usually just threw it in a bun. Honestly, I wasn't one of the popular kids back then.

**That's hard to believe.**
It's true—they called me "Olive Oyl." I was awkwardly tall, towering over every guy in my grade. Not exactly a flattering look at the time.

**So how did you transform your look since then?**
Skincare is everything, starting with sunscreen as the non-negotiable basic. I've stuck with Oil of Olay daytime moisturizer since childhood, following my mom's example—their foaming cleanser doubles as an amazing makeup remover too. Each morning I use Olay's Age Defying Daily Renewal cleanser because those tiny exfoliating beads work wonders. Whenever people compliment my complexion, I just laugh and think, "Lucky for me, I'm not blowing $150 on fancy products." Sure, high-end skincare probably works great, but why mess with something that's already working?

# The Beauty Evolution of Brooke Burns

At 29, Brooke Burns has come a long way from her early experiments with makeup—though she remembers those days vividly. As a 9-year-old aspiring ballerina, she wasn't afraid to go bold, raiding her mom's makeup drawer for a swipe of red lipstick and pairing it with drugstore black eyeliner. It was a dramatic look for a little girl, but one that clearly left an impression, shaping her lifelong relationship with cosmetics.

Now a single mother herself, Burns has adopted a very different philosophy when it comes to her own 7-year-old daughter's introduction to makeup. Rather than discouraging her daughter's interest altogether, she's taken a pragmatic approach, teaching her the "a dab'll do ya" method—a lighter, more subtle application than her own childhood experiments. Her reasoning is simple and refreshingly realistic: her daughter is going to wear makeup one way or another, so she might as well guide her toward a more tasteful, understated technique from the start.

Professionally, Burns has picked up plenty of tricks from her time in the modeling world, and she's happy to share them. One of her go-to techniques involves using a white pencil along the inner bottom eyelid, an easy way to brighten the eyes and create the illusion of being more awake and refreshed. For nighttime, she keeps things simple but effective, relying on just mascara and black pencil to create a quick, sultry eye look without much fuss.

When it comes to foundation, Burns is loyal to Revlon Color Stay, praising its impressive longevity throughout the day, built-in sunscreen for added protection, and its ability to give her skin a natural, healthy glow rather than a mask-like finish.

Her hair color has also evolved over the years. These days, Burns favors being a brunette, explaining that when she was blond, the combination with her already big, vivacious personality made her come across as somewhat glib or superficial. # Brooke Burns: My Beauty Evolution, From Red Lipstick to Raising a Daughter

Growing up, I was obsessed with makeup in the way only a little girl can be. I remember sneaking into my mother's bathroom and finding this bold, red lipstick—the kind that felt so grown-up and glamorous. I'd swipe it on way outside the lines of my lips, thinking I looked like a movie star, when really I probably looked like I'd been in a fight with a marker. But that's the beauty of being a kid; you experiment without any real understanding of technique or subtlety. You just want to feel beautiful and bold.

Fast forward to now, and I find myself on the other side of that experience—teaching my own daughter about makeup, but with a very different philosophy. Where I once reached for the boldest red I could find, I'm now showing her the beauty of subtlety. We talk about how less is often more, especially when you're young. I want her to understand that makeup can enhance her natural features rather than mask them. We practice with soft pinks and sheer glosses, and I explain why a little goes a long way. It's funny how full circle that experience has become—from being the child smearing lipstick everywhere to being the mother gently guiding my own daughter through her first makeup lessons.

My modeling career taught me so much about the practical side of beauty—the tricks that actually work when you're under pressure, whether that's a photo shoot with tight timing or an early morning call time. One thing I learned quickly was how to fake a good night's sleep even when I hadn't gotten one. There's a trick where you use a bit of white or light-colored eyeliner on your waterline—it instantly opens up your eyes and makes you look more awake and refreshed. It's such a simple thing, but it makes such a dramatic difference, especially when you're running on four hours of sleep and a lot of coffee.

Another lesson from my modeling days was learning to find products that actually deliver, rather than just relying on brand hype. My go-to foundation is one I've stuck with for years now because it never lets me down—it gives me that perfect, natural-looking coverage without feeling heavy or cakey. It's become such a staple in my routine that I genuinely feel like something's missing on my face without it. When you find something that works that well for your skin, you learn to hold onto it.

Beyond the makeup itself, though, there's something I've come to feel really strongly about when it comes to my hair color, and it's not what people always expect. I've dyed my hair various shades throughout my career, but I keep coming back to dark hair, and there's actually a very specific reason why. When I'm blonde, I notice something shifts in how people perceive me—there's this unspoken assumption that comes along with it, like I'm somehow more "glib" or less serious. It's such a strange thing to put into words, but going lighter seems to invite people to focus less on what I'm actually saying or doing, and more on some stereotype they've attached to blonde hair.

When my hair is dark, though, I feel like people actually look at my face and listen to what I'm saying. It draws attention to my personality and my expressions rather than to some preconceived notion about hair color. There's something about dark hair that seems to ground people's perception of me—it feels more authentic to who I actually am, and it allows my actual personality to come through in interactions rather than getting overshadowed by assumptions.

It's fascinating how much something as simple as hair color can shape public perception throughout a career. I've experienced it firsthand—the shift in how people approach conversations with me, the types of roles I've been considered for, even the way interviews have gone based on whether I was blonde or brunette at the time. It's made me really conscious of the choices I make with my appearance, understanding that they're not just personal preferences but actually have real implications for how I'm perceived professionally and personally. 

At the end of the day, though, whether it's teaching my daughter about subtle makeup application, sharing the tricks I picked up from years of modeling, or making decisions about my hair color, it all comes back to the same thing for me: authenticity. I want to look and feel like myself, and I want the choices I make about my appearance to actually serve who I am, rather than working against it.

# Brooke Burns Gets Real About Her Beauty Routine, Hair Color Confessions, and the One Product She'll Never Skip

The actress and former game show host opens up about aging gracefully, her decades-long relationship with sunscreen, and why she's not afraid to admit she gets Botox.

---

There's a certain effortlessness to Brooke Burns that feels almost unfair. The actress—known for *Baywatch*, *Dog Eat Dog*, and a string of TV movies—has spent over two decades in front of cameras that don't miss a pore. When we catch up with her over Zoom, she's makeup-free save for a swipe of tinted lip balm, and her skin has that lit-from-within quality that no amount of ring light can fake.

"I think people assume I have this elaborate routine because of my job, but honestly, I've gotten more low-maintenance as I've gotten older," Burns says, laughing. "I used to layer on so much product in my twenties. Now I'm like, less is more, please."

Here, Burns breaks down her go-to makeup look, the wild history of her hair color, and the skincare rule she's followed since she was a teenager.

**On her everyday makeup routine:**

"I'm a tinted moisturizer girl through and through. I don't wear foundation unless it's for a shoot or a red carpet. My morning routine is tinted moisturizer, cream blush—I like to apply it with my fingers so it looks like it's coming from within—and then a really good brow gel because my brows have gotten sparser with age, nobody talks about that enough. Mascara, always. And then a lip balm or gloss. That's it. That's the whole face most days."

"If I'm doing something more, I'll add a bronzer, maybe a little eyeliner smudged along the lash line. But I've learned that the more makeup I put on, the older I actually look. It's counterintuitive but true."

**On the products she'd never travel without:**

"A good concealer for under-eyes—non-negotiable, I have two kids and a full life, the eye bags are real. And SPF lip balm. I picked that habit up from my mom and I've never stopped."

**On her hair color evolution:**

Burns is candid about her hair history, which has run the gamut from beachy blonde to darker, richer tones over the years. "I've been every shade of blonde that exists," she says. "Platinum in my twenties, which I regret because it fried my hair. Honey blonde for years because of *Baywatch* and just, you know, the whole California thing. Then I went through a phase in my thirties where I wanted to look 'taken seriously' so I went darker, more of an ash brown."

"Now I've landed somewhere I actually love—a dimensional blonde with lowlights instead of just going lighter and lighter. It's lower maintenance, and it makes my eyes pop more than the platinum ever did. Also, I finally started using purple shampoo religiously, which I ignored for years and shouldn't have."

She adds: "I will say, I've dyed my hair so many times that I'm now obsessed with bond-building treatments. If I skip them, my ends just say no."

**On her skincare secrets:**

"SPF. I know everyone says it, but I mean it—I've worn sunscreen on my face every single day since I was probably fifteen. I grew up around the beach, I saw what sun damage does. That's the number one thing."

"Beyond that, I'm a big believer in simplicity. I use a gentle cleanser, a vitamin C serum in the morning, retinol at night a few times a week, and a rich moisturizer. I don't overdo actives because I think people burn out their skin barrier trying every trending ingredient at once."

"I also get facials when I can, and yes—I'll say it—I get Botox. Not a ton, just enough to soften things. I think there's this weird pressure to pretend you don't do anything, and I'd rather just be honest about it. I'm 46, I've lived a life, and I want to look like myself, just rested."

**On the beauty advice she'd give her younger self:**

"Wear sunscreen even more than you think you need to, and stop picking at your skin. Also, stop bleaching your hair within an inch of its life—just trust me on that one."

---

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.*

# Beauty Confessions: Brooke Burns Spills Her Drugstore Favorites and Childhood Makeup Memories

There's something refreshingly relatable about a celebrity who admits she still raids the drugstore aisles for her go-to beauty products. Brooke Burns, known for her work in film and television, recently sat down to chat about her beauty routine, and it turns out her secrets aren't locked away in some exclusive boutique—they're sitting right there on the shelf at your local pharmacy.

**Q: Let's start with the basics. Do you have a drugstore beauty product you can't live without?**

Brooke Burns: Honestly, yes, and I'm not just saying that to sound down-to-earth. I've tried every high-end mascara you can imagine, but I always find myself circling back to drugstore formulas. There's something about the affordability that makes me less precious about it too—I'll actually use it up instead of babying it in a drawer.

**Q: What is it about drugstore products that keeps you coming back?**

Burns: They just work! I think sometimes we assume that a higher price tag means better quality, but that's not always true. Some of the most effective formulas—for skin, for lips, for eyes—are the ones that have been on shelves for decades. They're tried and true. Plus, I'm a busy mom, and running into a drugstore to grab something is just easier than making a special trip somewhere else.

**Q: Is there a product you've been loyal to for years?**

Burns: Definitely. There's a classic drugstore lip balm that I've used since I was a teenager. It's nostalgic at this point. Whenever I put it on, I'm brought right back to being a kid getting ready for a school dance or something. It's silly, but beauty products can really transport you like that.

**Q: Speaking of being a kid, what's your earliest makeup memory?**

Burns: Oh, this is a good one. I remember sneaking into my mom's makeup bag when I was maybe seven or eight. I found this bright blue eyeshadow—so '80s—and I put it on so thick, like I was trying to audition for a costume party. My mom walked in and just started laughing. She wasn't mad, she just couldn't believe how confident I looked wearing something so outrageous.

**Q: Did that experience shape your relationship with makeup later on?**

Burns: I think so! It taught me early on that makeup is supposed to be fun. It's not this serious, high-stakes thing—it's playful. Even now, when I'm doing my makeup for a red carpet or a shoot, I try to remember that feeling of just experimenting without fear.

**Q: Any other childhood beauty memories that stick with you?**

Burns: My grandmother used to let me sit with her while she did her makeup before church on Sundays. She had this beautiful vanity with a big mirror, and she'd let me dab a little of her powder on my face, very lightly, of course. It felt so special and grown-up. I think that's where my love for the whole ritual of beauty really started—not just the products, but the experience of it.

**Q: Do you pass any of these memories or routines on to your own kids?**

Burns: Absolutely. My daughter loves to sit with me while I get ready, and I let her play with some kid-safe, washable makeup. It's become our little bonding time, much like it was for me with my grandmother. I want her to see makeup as something joyful, not something you need to be perfect at.

**Q: Last question—if you had to recommend just one drugstore product to our readers, what would it be?**

Burns: I'd have to say a good drugstore tinted moisturizer or BB cream. It's such an easy, no-fuss way to even out your skin without looking overly done. Perfect for busy days when you want to look put-together but don't have hours to spend on your face.

---

Brooke Burns proves that great beauty doesn't have to come with a luxury price tag—and that some of our best beauty memories start with a little mischief in mom's makeup bag.

# Beauty & Balance: A Conversation with Brooke Burns

*From the pages of Radiance Monthly*

---

**RM: Let's start at the beginning. You trained as a ballerina before your career took you elsewhere. How did that discipline shape the way you think about beauty today?**

**Brooke Burns:** Ballet was really my first education in body awareness and self-discipline. You learn to appreciate what your body can do, not just how it looks in a mirror. That perspective stuck with me. Beauty isn't static—it's connected to movement, posture, how you carry yourself. Even now, I catch myself thinking about alignment when I'm just walking through a room. Dancers also learn early that maintenance is daily and unglamorous. You don't get to skip stretching because you're tired. I think that translates directly into skincare and self-care as an adult—consistency over intensity.

**RM: Did that dancer's discipline follow you into your skincare routine?**

**Brooke Burns:** Completely. I'm not someone who does elaborate ten-step routines. I'd rather do five things really well, every single day, than twenty things sporadically. Ballet taught me that repetition is what creates results—not a single grand gesture.

**RM: Speaking of routines, walk us through your current skincare regimen.**

**Brooke Burns:** Mornings are simple: a gentle cleanser, a vitamin C serum, moisturizer, and SPF—non-negotiable, even in winter. I learned the hard way in my twenties that sun damage doesn't announce itself until years later. At night, I double cleanse if I've had makeup on, then I use a retinol a few nights a week, followed by a heavier night cream. I also love facial oils—rosehip or squalane—especially as I've gotten older and my skin needs more hydration than it used to.

**RM: Any products you consider holy grail?**

**Brooke Burns:** A good vitamin C serum is essential—it brightens and protects. And honestly, a great SPF is the single best anti-aging product anyone can buy. I'm loyal to a few skincare brands, but I also believe in rotating based on what your skin needs seasonally.

**RM: How has your approach to beauty evolved as you've gotten older?**

**Brooke Burns:** In my twenties, beauty felt performative—like something you did for other people. Now it feels more like self-respect. I care less about looking a certain way and more about looking like a well-rested, healthy version of myself. I've also become much more interested in what's going on internally—sleep, hydration, stress management—because it shows up on your skin faster than any product will fix.

**RM: Do you have a wellness philosophy that ties into your beauty routine?**

**Brooke Burns:** Beauty starts from the inside out, and I don't mean that in a cliché way. Drinking enough water, moving your body, managing stress—all of that shows up on your face. I still incorporate movement daily, even if it's not ballet anymore. Pilates, long walks, stretching—things that keep my body feeling connected and aligned, the way dance did.

**RM: Any advice for readers who feel overwhelmed by the beauty industry's constant trends?**

**Brooke Burns:** Simplify. Find the basics that work for your skin and stick with them. Trends come and go, but consistency is what actually changes your skin over time. And give yourself grace—beauty should feel like self-care, not another job.

**RM: Last question—what does beauty mean to you today?**

**Brooke Burns:** Confidence, ease, and taking care of yourself without obsessing over perfection. That's a lesson dance taught me long before skincare did: show up, do the work, and trust the process.

# Brooke Burns: On High School Insecurities, Hair Battles, and Her $12 Skincare Secret

*By InStyle Staff*

There's something instantly disarming about Brooke Burns. Maybe it's the sun-kissed California ease she's carried since her *Baywatch* days, or maybe it's her refreshing willingness to admit that glamour has never come without a fight. Over coffee (oat milk latte, extra hot), the actress and former game show host opens up about the awkward-phase memories that still make her cringe, her decades-long hair saga, and the drugstore products she'll defend to the death.

## "I Was the Tallest Kid in Every Class Photo"

Before the red carpets and swimsuit shoots, Burns says she was an awkward teenager who felt anything but confident. "I hit 5'9" by ninth grade and I felt like a giraffe walking through the halls," she laughs. "I used to hunch my shoulders trying to seem shorter. It's wild looking back now, wishing I could tell that girl to just stand up straight and own it."

She also recalls a particularly mortifying home-perm incident sophomore year. "My mom thought it would be fun to save money and do it ourselves. I walked into homeroom looking like a poodle who'd stuck her paw in a socket. I wore a baseball cap for two weeks straight."

## The Hair Struggle Is Real

Speaking of hair—Burns says her relationship with her strands has been complicated for most of her adult life. "I have this frustrating combination of fine texture but a ton of it," she explains. "Stylists get so excited and then twenty minutes in they're like, 'oh... okay, this is going to take a while.'"

Years of on-camera blowouts and beachy waves for *Baywatch* took their toll. "I fried my hair so many times in my twenties chasing that surfer-girl look. Eventually I had to take a step back, cut things shorter, and let it breathe."

Her current holy grail? A weekly deep-conditioning ritual she does herself. "I'm not precious about salon treatments anymore. I mix a drugstore hair mask with a few drops of argan oil, pile it on, and sit under a shower cap for thirty minutes while I answer emails."

## Skincare That Won't Break the Bank

Despite years in an industry obsessed with luxury, Burns is refreshingly loyal to budget-friendly staples. "People assume I've got some elaborate ten-step routine with serums that cost more than my rent used to," she jokes. "Honestly? I'm a creature of habit, and cheap stuff works."

Her non-negotiables:

- **CeraVe Foaming Facial Cleanser** ($12): "I've used this for years. It doesn't strip my skin, and I always have a backup bottle under the sink."
- **Aquaphor Healing Ointment** ($9): "For dry patches, cuticles, chapped lips—everything. My kids think it's hilarious how much I love this stuff."
- **Neutrogena Hydro Boost Water Gel** ($19): "It's lightweight enough for daytime but still gives me that plump, dewy thing everyone's chasing."
- **La Roche-Posay Anthelios SPF** ($36, her one splurge): "Non-negotiable. I learned the sun-damage lesson the hard way from all those years filming near the water."

## Confidence, Reframed

Looking back at her high school insecurities and the hair mishaps that followed her into adulthood, Burns says the throughline has been learning to laugh at herself. "I think we put so much pressure on getting it 'right'—the perfect hair, the perfect skin. But some of my favorite memories are from the messiest moments. That poodle perm? I'd never do it again, but I also wouldn't erase it."

She pauses, smiling. "Confidence isn't about looking flawless. It's about being able to tell the story about the time you didn't."
